title: Foundations
tagline: Refresh core PM principles — problem validation, then value, viability, feasibility, and usability — reframed for AI.
intro: Before applying an AI lens to anything, it's worth refreshing the general principles that hold regardless of AI: know which part of the PM job you're actually doing, and validate the problem before you validate the solution. Below: a quick refresher on where this program focuses, then problem validation, then the classic value/viability/feasibility/usability lens — each with the one AI-specific question it now hides.

diagram.caption: The Pragmatic Framework splits PM work into Strategy (Market, Focus, Business) and Execution (Planning, Programs, Enablement, Support). This program builds fluency for the Strategy half — the problem-validation and solution-scoring judgment calls below — since that's where AI most changes what one PM can sustain.

scenario.context: Meridian Logistics (a fictional 3,400-employee trucking and logistics company) is a customer of Equifax's Onboarding product category — which includes I-9, E-Verify, Onboarding Forms, and WOTC — and specifically uses the I-9 product. Federal law requires a new hire to complete Section 1 of Form I-9 by their first day of work, and requires Meridian's HR team to complete Section 2 — examining the new hire's identity and work-authorization documents — within 3 business days of that start date. Meridian's HR team does that examination by hand today, checking each new hire's documents against the accepted List A (identity + work authorization in one document) or List B plus List C (identity and work authorization as two separate documents) combinations — a process prone to missed 3-day deadlines and inconsistent checks across a high-volume, high-turnover workforce.
scenario.brief: Feature idea under review: an AI I-9 Completion Assistant that reads a new hire's submitted Section 1 fields and List A/B/C document images, flags anything inconsistent or missing before the 3-business-day Section 2 deadline, and drafts a note for the HR admin explaining exactly what it found. A human HR admin reviews and approves every flag — and completes Section 2 — before anything reaches the employee.

sections.heading: Problem Validation
sections.learning: Before scoring a solution, validate that the problem is worth solving at all — with or without AI. The classic test: is it urgent (does it hurt enough, right now, that people will act), pervasive (does it affect enough people to matter), and is there a genuine willingness to buy (will someone pay — in money, time, or switching cost — to have it solved)? A problem missing even one of the three is a weak foundation, no matter how good the eventual solution is.

example.text: Missed I-9 deadlines and inconsistent document checks are urgent (a missed 3-business-day deadline is real compliance exposure, not a someday problem), pervasive (every one of Meridian's ~40 weekly new hires goes through this, at every one of its dozen sites), and backed by a clear willingness to buy — Meridian already pays Equifax specifically for its I-9 product to reduce this risk, so this isn't a hard sell.

sections.pitfall: Skipping straight to 'AI could help with this' without checking urgency and pervasiveness first. A problem that's rare or low-stakes doesn't become worth solving just because AI makes a solution technically possible.

field.label: Your turn: Problem validation
field.help: Is the I-9 compliance problem urgent, pervasive, and something Meridian is willing to pay to solve?
field.placeholder: Assess urgency, pervasiveness, and willingness to buy — not the solution yet, just the problem.

sections.heading: Value
sections.learning: With the problem validated, turn to the solution. Is AI the right mechanism here, or would a simpler tool — a deadline-tracking checklist, say — solve this just as well? AI is worth it when the judgment involved is genuinely hard to encode as rules; it's overkill when a simple form would do (compare a straightforward eligibility-matching tool like WOTC screening — a sibling product in the same Onboarding category — where rules alone often get you most of the way).

example.text: Meridian's HR team handles roughly 40 new hires a week across a dozen sites. A checklist alone won't catch inconsistent handwriting between Section 1 and a List B or C document, or a document that's technically present but expired — exactly the errors that trigger missed 3-business-day deadlines. Reading and cross-checking documents is a judgment call a rules checklist can't make; that's where AI earns its place here.

sections.pitfall: Treating 'AI can do this' as the same claim as 'AI should do this.' If a fixed rule — is the SSN nine digits, is a required field blank — would catch the error just as reliably, building an AI feature for it only adds cost and a new failure mode without adding judgment.

field.label: Your turn: Value
field.help: Is AI the right mechanism for the I-9 Completion Assistant, or would something simpler work as well?
field.placeholder: State the judgment call AI is making here that a simpler tool couldn't.

sections.heading: Viability
sections.learning: Classic viability asks whether the business case closes. AI viability adds a cost that scales with usage — every model call has a marginal cost. A feature that's cheap to build can still be expensive to run at scale, and you now have a build-vs-buy-vs-prompt decision: fine-tune a model, call a vendor API, or just write a very good prompt against an existing model.

example.text: At Meridian's volume (~40 new hires/week, roughly 2-3 documents each), per-document inference cost is small next to the HR-hours saved on manual review. A well-prompted existing model should be sufficient to start — no fine-tuning needed until we have a large enough set of flagged/unflagged outcomes to justify it.

sections.pitfall: Estimating cost off a demo instead of real volume. A feature that costs pennies per call in testing can add up fast once every one of Meridian's ~40 weekly hires runs 2-3 documents through it, every week, indefinitely — model the cost at 6-12 months of real volume, not day one.

field.label: Your turn: Viability
field.help: What does this cost to run at Meridian's volume, and is prompting an existing model enough, or does this need something heavier?
field.placeholder: Estimate the scale, and name the build-vs-buy-vs-prompt call.

sections.heading: Feasibility
sections.learning: Feasibility used to mostly mean engineering capacity. Now it also means: do we have the data this needs, and is it clean enough to use? Can the model reliably do this task at all? Eval-driven development means defining your success criteria and test cases before you build, not writing a rubric after something ships and looks wrong.

example.text: Federal I-9 requirements are well documented and stable (the Form I-9 instructions and the accompanying M-274 Handbook for Employers), and Meridian is already required to retain every completed I-9 for 3 years after hire, or 1 year after termination, whichever is later — so there's a real historical corpus to test against, not just a handful of examples. Before trusting this in production, we'd run the assistant against 100 historical Meridian I-9 packets with known outcomes (approved, corrected via a receipt, rejected) and check it flags the same issues an HR admin already caught — without inventing new ones.

sections.pitfall: Treating 'it worked on the examples I tried' as proof. A handful of clean cases will pass almost any model — the real test is the messy 10%: an expired List C document, a receipt for a lost document, borderline handwriting. If your test set skips those, you haven't tested the part that actually breaks.

field.label: Your turn: Feasibility
field.help: Is the data ready, and how would you prove this works before shipping it?
field.placeholder: Name the test set you'd build and what 'passing' would look like.

sections.heading: Usability
sections.learning: Every AI feature will sometimes be wrong. Usability now includes: does the user know when to trust the output? Is there a graceful way to correct it? An AI feature with no visible 'this might be wrong, here's how to fix it' path is a usability gap, not just an accuracy gap.

example.text: Every flag the assistant raises shows the specific I-9 field and the federal rule it's checking against, so an HR admin can verify at a glance instead of taking it on faith. Anything involving a document type the model hasn't seen before, or a new hire flagged in a prior audit, routes to manual review instead of an automated flag.

sections.pitfall: Designing the happy path and forgetting the correction path. The moment an HR admin disagrees with a flag and has no clear way to say so — and have that disagreement recorded — is the moment they stop trusting the tool entirely, even if it's right 95% of the time.

field.label: Your turn: Usability
field.help: How does an HR admin know when to trust a flag versus double-check it? What's the correction path?
field.placeholder: Describe how trust is shown, and what triggers a human-only path.
